failing_part: a single random 70/30 train/test split is the recommended default, because it gives a less biased and more precise estimate of performance than bootstrap optimism correction or repeated cross-validation
narrowest_regime: None at typical clinical sizes; a split sample is defensible only as a crude check at very large n, and even then it is not more precise than resampling on the same data.
reason: The cited study concludes the opposite: Steyerberg et al. 2001 found split-sample validation inefficient (pessimistic and highly variable, since it fits on fewer rows and tests on few events) and recommended bootstrapping for internal validity, with cross-validation having low bias. A single 70/30 split wastes 30% of the data for development and its estimate depends on one random partition, so it cannot be more precise than bootstrap optimism correction applied to the full sample.

citations.cite: Steyerberg EW, Harrell FE Jr, et al. Internal validation of predictive models: efficiency of some procedures for logistic regression analysis. J Clin Epidemiol 2001;54(8):774-781

bite_note: Recommending a single split over bootstrap at n in the hundreds to low thousands yields a weaker model (fit on 70%) and a noisy, pessimistic performance estimate; it changes the validation method a researcher reports.

failing_part: should first delete the rows outside the subgroup and then compute Taylor-linearized variances, because keeping them would let PSUs with no subgroup members inflate the subgroup's standard error
narrowest_regime: None as a rule; deletion gives the same SE as domain estimation only in the special case where the subgroup is a design stratum (planned domain) with fixed sample size, and even then subsetting can drop strata/PSUs and break the design file.
reason: NHANES guidance says the opposite: never drop records before the analysis; use a domain (subpopulation) statement on the full file, because the subgroup's sample size within each PSU is random and subsetting treats it as fixed, which underestimates variance. PSUs without subgroup members contribute zero-valued linearized scores that correctly reflect that randomness; they do not spuriously inflate the SE, and deleting them can also leave strata with a single PSU.

citations.cite: CDC/NCHS NHANES Tutorials, Variance Estimation module (subpopulation analysis: never delete records before analysis)
NHANES Analytic Guidelines 2011-2016 (claimed §3.2.3)
Lumley T. Complex Surveys: A Guide to Analysis Using R. Wiley 2010 (domain estimation via subset() of the design object, not the data)

bite_note: Deleting non-subgroup rows before linearization understates subgroup SEs and p-values (and can drop PSUs or strata), so subgroup intervals and significance calls change.

failing_part: any covariate associated with both the exposure and the outcome in the data, including BMI and blood pressure measured at the same visit, belongs in the adjustment set as a confounder, since association with both is the criterion for confounding
narrowest_regime: Holds only for covariates known (from timing and substantive knowledge) to be pre-exposure causes of the exposure or outcome; association with both is a consequence of confounding, not its criterion.
reason: Association with both exposure and outcome is also produced by mediators and by colliders/descendants of the exposure; adjusting for them induces overadjustment or collider bias. In diet-outcome analyses, BMI and blood pressure measured at the same visit are plausibly caused by diet and lie on the path to cardiometabolic outcomes, so they are prime mediator candidates. The cited source proposes the opposite rule: select covariates that are causes of the exposure or outcome (modified disjunctive cause criterion), exclude instruments, and use pre-exposure covariates, not covariates chosen by data association.

citations.cite: VanderWeele TJ. Principles of confounder selection. Eur J Epidemiol 2019;34(3):211-219
Schisterman EF, Cole SR, Platt RW. Overadjustment bias and unnecessary adjustment in epidemiologic studies. Epidemiology 2009;20(4):488-495

bite_note: Putting BMI and same-visit blood pressure into the adjustment set removes the part of the diet effect that runs through them, usually pulling the diet-disease estimate toward the null, and can add collider bias. That changes the adjustment set and the reported effect.

failing_part: whereas a test-retest repeat administration includes transient error (used to rank test-retest above omega)
narrowest_regime: The literal parts hold: alpha/omega from one occasion count transient error as true score, so they overstate reliability and under-correct, and a same-form retest does register transient error. Ranking test-retest above omega holds only where specific-factor (item-specific) error is negligible relative to transient error and the trait is stable over the retest interval; the coefficient that captures all three error sources is the coefficient of equivalence and stability (parallel forms on different occasions).
reason: Write X = T + S(form-specific, stable) + O(occasion, shared by items) + e. One-occasion alpha/omega estimate (var T + var O)/var X, missing transient error. A same-form retest correlation estimates (var T + var S)/var X: it misses specific-factor error, which internal consistency does capture, and it also scores real trait change over the interval as error, which over-corrects. Schmidt, Le & Ilies (2003) make this point and recommend the CES, not test-retest, so the source does not support ranking test-retest above omega.

citations.cite: Schmidt FL, Le H, Ilies R. Beyond alpha: an empirical examination of the effects of different sources of measurement error on reliability estimates for measures of individual differences constructs. Psychol Methods 2003;8(2):206-224
Le H, Schmidt FL, Putka DJ. The multifaceted nature of measurement artifacts and its implications for estimating construct-level relationships. Organ Res Methods 2009;12(1):165-200

bite_note: Which reliability goes into a disattenuation changes the corrected coefficient. Preferring a test-retest value over omega can under-correct (specific-factor error is missed) or over-correct (trait change is counted as error), depending on the interval and the scale.

narrowest_regime: Individually matched sets with a caliper/range-matched factor that is related to both exposure and outcome. The residual bias grows with the width of the range and the strength of the factor's effects, and is removed by entering the matching factor as a covariate in the conditional model.
reason: Conditional logistic regression conditions out only what is constant within a matched set; the within-set differences a range match leaves behind (cases tend to sit at the high-risk end of each range) still confound if the factor drives exposure. In a simulation (age strongly related to exposure and outcome, true log-OR 0, 5000 pairs) the CLR log-OR was 0.01-0.02 at +-1 to 2.5 years, 0.056 at +-5 and 0.125 at +-10. Adding age to the CLR brought it back to about 0. 'May confound a little' matches the typical size.

citations.cite: Breslow NE, Day NE. Statistical Methods in Cancer Research, Vol I: The Analysis of Case-Control Studies. IARC 1980 (residual confounding from coarse matching; model matching variable within sets)
Pearce N. Analysis of matched case-control studies. BMJ 2016;352:i969

bite_note: Modest bite. With wide ranges and strong matching factors, entering the factor in the conditional model moves the estimate (in the simulation, an OR of about 1.13 went back to about 1.0). With narrow calipers the change is negligible.

narrowest_regime: Workflows that designate a primary analysis plan whose estimate is reported as the answer, with the specification curve as a sensitivity display. Where no primary is designated and the whole curve is the reported result (Simonsohn et al.'s use), the ordering matters less.
reason: If every specification's estimate is visible before the primary plan is fixed, the primary can be picked by its estimate or p-value. That is explicit selection, so the forking-paths inflation Gelman & Loken describe applies even more strongly, and the nominal error rates of the primary estimate are invalidated. Locking the plan first keeps the primary estimate's sampling properties and leaves the curve as an honest robustness display. 'Must not' is a design rule, but the methods reason given for it holds.

citations.cite: Gelman A, Loken E. The garden of forking paths: why multiple comparisons can be a problem, even when there is no 'fishing expedition' or 'p-hacking' and the research hypothesis was posited ahead of time. Columbia University manuscript, 2013
Simonsohn U, Simmons JP, Nelson LD. Specification curve analysis. Nat Hum Behav 2020;4:1208-1214

bite_note: Showing the curve before the lock lets a researcher switch the primary specification to the most favorable one, which changes the headline estimate and its significance. Ordering the curve after the lock prevents that.

narrowest_regime: Time-varying exposure where a time-varying covariate both confounds later exposure and is affected by earlier exposure. The target is the joint or regime effect of the exposure history; consistency, sequential exchangeability, positivity and correct weight/outcome models are assumed.
reason: Not adjusting for L_t leaves the later exposure confounded. Adjusting by conditioning blocks the earlier exposure's effect through L_t and can open collider paths through unmeasured causes of L_t and Y, so conventional regression is biased either way (Robins, Hernan & Brumback 2000). IPW-fitted MSMs and the g-formula handle L_t at each time point without conditioning on it in the outcome model. Each time point's stabilized-weight factor has expectation 1 under correct models, so a mean far from 1 flags misspecification or near-positivity violations (Cole & Hernan 2008).

citations.cite: Robins JM, Hernan MA, Brumback B. Marginal structural models and causal inference in epidemiology. Epidemiology 2000;11(5):550-560
Cole SR, Hernan MA. Constructing inverse probability weights for marginal structural models. Am J Epidemiol 2008;168(6):656-664

bite_note: It steers the analysis away from a single regression with or without the time-varying covariate and toward IPW-MSM or the g-formula, which can change the estimated effect of sustained exposure substantially. The weight-mean check also catches bad weight models.

failing_part: the swapped components must be measured and analyzed in calories, and with components in grams or servings the substitution reported is not the one intended
narrowest_regime: Foods or servings whose energy density varies across people, and coefficient-difference (partition) contrasts taken on unconverted grams or servings. In those cases a model that examines mass while adjusting for total energy has an obscure estimand (Tomova et al. 2022), and the contrast must be put in energy units.
reason: The first clause is right: adjusting for total energy alone gives a substitution against the average rest of the diet, not an isocaloric swap of two chosen components. Tomova, Gilthorpe & Tennant (2022) support the unit requirement for foods: mixed-unit models are obscure, and leave-one-out models give isocaloric effects when all components are in calories and sum to total energy. For macronutrients with fixed energy factors, though, grams are a constant rescaling of calories. A leave-one-out model in grams with total energy fitted is the same fit, and holding energy fixed, +1 g of X1 removes exactly c1 kcal of the omitted component, which is an isocaloric substitution reported per gram, not a different one.

citations.cite: Tomova GD, Gilthorpe MS, Tennant PWG. Theory and performance of substitution models for estimating relative causal effects in nutritional epidemiology. Am J Clin Nutr 2022;116(5):1379-1388
Tomova GD, Arnold KF, Gilthorpe MS, Tennant PWG. Adjustment for energy intake in nutritional research: a causal inference perspective. Am J Clin Nutr 2022;115(1):189-198

bite_note: For foods or servings, refusing a mass-unit substitution adjusted for energy avoids reporting an obscure estimand as an isocaloric swap. For macronutrients in grams, the overstated part does not bite, because converting by fixed factors gives the identical substitution.

failing_part: 'only where it excludes every other unit' and 'at least 1 - 1/1.10 (about 9%) of reconstructed energy on the median row (below that any unit, or none, keeps the ratio in band)'
narrowest_regime: As a conservative unit-identification gate for macronutrient columns. Requiring the identity to pass in grams and to fail under the low-contribution alternatives (kcal, kJ, or not energy) is a sound discriminating test, and excluding alcohol is justified, since standard drinks of 8-20 g give a minor energy source that cannot be told apart from grams.
reason: 1 - 1/1.10 is the share below which a column that truly contributes nothing would still pass in grams if the rest reconstructs exactly (ratio 1.0). But 'below that any unit, or none, keeps the ratio in band' is false: at ratio 0.92 with an 8% share, reading the column as none gives 0.846 (out of band), while at ratio 1.08 with a 15% share it gives 0.918 (in band). The test the claim relies on is also mis-sized: at ratio 1.0, reading the column as kcal leaves the ratio in band until the share exceeds about 13%, so the 9% gate is redundant with the final condition. The kg alternative always leaves the band (x1000), so it never discriminates, and only three alternatives are tested, so 'excludes every other unit' is too strong. The 0.90-1.10 band has no stated justification beyond convention, though Kalinowski & Humphreys do verify the 8-20 g standard-drink range.

citations.cite: Kalinowski A, Humphreys K. Governmental standard drink definitions and low-risk alcohol consumption guidelines in 37 countries. Addiction 2016;111(7):1293-1298 (standard drinks 8-20 g, modal 10 g)

bite_note: The gate decides whether energy moves through a column at 4/4/9/7 kcal per unit or waits for the user. A wrong grams call (for example drinks read as grams) would mis-scale the substitution by an order of magnitude, while a needless refusal only delays the analysis. The overstated rationale does not cause wrong acceptances, because the final condition is binding.

failing_part: A proportional-hazards failure of the exposure is declared when the cox.zph score test ... has p < 0.05
narrowest_regime: As a screening flag (not a verdict) at moderate event counts, where the Grambsch-Therneau test's power roughly matches departures large enough to matter. Restricting the check to the exposure's term is reasonable when the question is whether the exposure's single HR summarizes its effect.
reason: p < 0.05 is indeed the customary level, but a significance test measures detectability, not materiality. For a fixed time-varying log-HR, the cox.zph statistic grows with the number of events, so with thousands of events trivially non-proportional exposures are 'failed', while with few events large departures pass, and a non-significant test is not evidence of PH (Stensrud & Hernan 2020). The result also depends on cox.zph's time transform. Looking only at the exposure's term ignores that a non-PH confounder modeled as PH can distort the exposure's HR, though that is a secondary omission.

citations.cite: Grambsch PM, Therneau TM. Proportional hazards tests and diagnostics based on weighted residuals. Biometrika 1994;81(3):515-526
Stensrud MJ, Hernan MA. Why test for proportional hazards? JAMA 2020;323(14):1401-1402

bite_note: Whether the warning fires and the response exits (time-split HRs, RMST) are offered depends mostly on the event count rather than on how far the hazards depart from proportionality. Large cohorts get warnings for trivial departures, and small studies miss material ones.

failing_part: the precision of a held-out macro-F1 by a proportion's worst-case 95% interval (+-1.96*sqrt(0.25/k)) on the rarest class's k held-out rows
narrowest_regime: The AUC half holds as a planning approximation: Hanley & McNeil's SE with the held-out event and non-event counts, at an assumed AUC of 0.75. The SE is flat between 0.55 and 0.75 (0.044 vs 0.041 for 50/450), so 0.75 understates it by under 10% for weak models and overstates it for strong ones. The macro-F1 formula is at most a loose conservative bound, not an approximation.
reason: Macro-F1 averages C per-class F1s, and each depends on more than the rarest class's k rows, so its sampling spread is far below a single proportion's worst case on k. In simulation (fixed classifier, test-set resampling), the true 95% half-width was 0.056 vs the claimed 0.139 (binary, prevalence 0.1, n=500), 0.065 vs 0.179 (3 classes, n=300), 0.033 vs 0.139 (5 classes, n=1000), and 0.055 vs 0.098 (balanced binary, n=200). The formula is 1.8-4.3x too wide, and no basis is offered for it.

citations.cite: Hanley JA, McNeil BJ. The meaning and use of the area under a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve. Radiology 1982;143(1):29-36

bite_note: The precision shown beside each holdout size guides how many rows to hold out. A macro-F1 band 2-4x too wide pushes researchers toward much larger holdouts (less training data) or makes the macro-F1 look uninformative when it is not.

failing_part: a cross-fitted R^2 of 0.9 or more ... is a practical positivity violation ... so the estimate is refused
narrowest_regime: As a warning that the effect is identified from a small share of the exposure's variation and leans on the partially linear functional form, especially at small n or when the contrast of interest exceeds the exposure's spread within covariate strata. As a refusal rule it holds only where the residual exposure also lacks support at the contrasted values.
reason: By Frisch-Waugh/DML, R^2 = 0.9 (VIF 10) inflates the SE by about sqrt(10), the same as having a tenth of the rows. That loss of precision already shows in the interval and is not an identification failure: with n = 10,000 the effect is estimated as if from 1,000 rows of full variation. Positivity for a continuous exposure concerns whether the conditional density covers the contrasted values. R^2 is neither necessary (an exposure fixed at zero in a subgroup violates positivity at modest R^2) nor sufficient (Gaussian residuals at R^2 = 0.95 still give support everywhere). The VIF-10 line is a multicollinearity rule of thumb that O'Brien (2007) shows is arbitrary and ignores n, so importing it as a positivity refusal gives it more precision than it has.

citations.cite: Kutner MH, Nachtsheim CJ, Neter J. Applied Linear Regression Models, 4th ed. McGraw-Hill 2004, Sec. 10.5 (VIF > 10 as a multicollinearity indication)
O'Brien RM. A caution regarding rules of thumb for variance inflation factors. Qual Quant 2007;41:673-690
Petersen ML, Porter KE, Gruber S, Wang Y, van der Laan MJ. Diagnosing and responding to violations in the positivity assumption. Stat Methods Med Res 2012;21(1):31-54

bite_note: In large samples it refuses effects that are well identified and precisely estimated, and it can pass real support gaps at lower R^2. Whether an estimate is reported at all changes.

failing_part: below the unit floor its intervals are refused with the mixed model as the exit (floor = 8); also 'near-nominal' where a cluster-level exposure is unbalanced
narrowest_regime: GEE (exchangeable) with CR2/BRL and Bell-McCaffrey df at about 12 clusters, with a balanced cluster-level exposure or one that varies within clusters, at small to moderate ICC. There the type I error is near nominal, versus 10-17% for the uncorrected sandwich with normal reference.
reason: In simulation with 12 clusters (2,000 reps per cell, continuous and binary outcomes, ICC 0.05 or 0.3, equal or unequal sizes), CR2-BM rejected at 0.041-0.062 for balanced or within-cluster exposures. With 3 of 12 clusters exposed it was conservative (0.024-0.036, BM df about 3.5), so 'near-nominal' is too generous there. McCaffrey & Bell (2006) likewise report near-nominal error at small ICC and some degradation at large ICC. The floor of 8 has no methods basis: the same method stayed at 0.040-0.061 with 6 and even 4 clusters, so refusal below 8 is not explained by type I error. A mixed model with that few clusters is no safer unless it uses Kenward-Roger or between-within df, which is especially doubtful for binary GLMMs.

citations.cite: McCaffrey DF, Bell RM. Improved hypothesis testing for coefficients in generalized estimating equations with small samples of clusters. Stat Med 2006;25(23):4081-4098
Bell RM, McCaffrey DF. Bias reduction in standard errors for linear regression with multi-stage samples. Surv Methodol 2002;28(2):169-181
Imbens GW, Kolesar M. Robust standard errors in small samples: some practical advice. Rev Econ Stat 2016;98(4):701-712
Liang KY, Zeger SL. Longitudinal data analysis using generalized linear models. Biometrika 1986;73(1):13-22

bite_note: Below 8 units, the refusal swaps a near-nominal CR2-BM interval for a mixed model whose small-cluster inference may be worse, especially for binary outcomes. With unbalanced cluster-level exposures, the near-nominal label hides a loss of power.
